extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) conducting/defending obviousness analyses under U.S. law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is obvious under 35 U.S.C. §103, including how to treat analogous art, motivation to combine, reasonable expectation of success, predictable results, teachings that teach away, lead compound issues, and weight to give secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference is 'analogous prior art' (and thus properly relied upon for an obviousness rejection) depends on whether it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention or is reasonably pertinent to the problem with which the inventor was involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of analogous art should be construed broadly (KSR). A reference that addresses the same problem or is reasonably pertinent to solving the problem can be analogous even if outside the inventor's exact field (examples: sealed padlock reference applied to tow-hitch lock; Teague bed folding mechanism applied to treadmills because both address retaining a folding mechanism). Office personnel should consider the problem to be solved in determining analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine / articulated reason(s) for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 must include an articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; mere conclusory statements are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Kahn / KSR: 'Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; instead, there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning.' (See MPEP § 2141). Office personnel must provide a reasoned explanation for every obviousness rejection and identify why a person of ordinary skill would have been led to combine references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recourse to common sense / logic in motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR permits consideration of logic, judgment, and common sense (in lieu of expert testimony) in the legal determination of obviousness; in appropriate cases the ultimate inference as to motivation to combine may 'boil down to a question of "common sense."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although common sense can support a finding of obviousness (and may be appropriate for summary judgment or JMOL), the examiner or tribunal should not end analysis solely with an invocation of common sense; the record should explain why a person of ordinary skill, in view of the facts, would have found the invention obvious (the Federal Circuit applied common sense but also explained the factual basis in Wyers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper obviousness determination includes whether there was a reasonable expectation of success in combining or modifying the prior art (In re O'Farrell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is not satisfied by a mere 'obvious to try' assertion absent a reasonable expectation of success. The level of skill in the art and the detailed teachings of the prior art bearing on predictability and enablement are relevant (examples: O'Farrell, Fout). 'Obviousness does not require absolute predictability of success.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (predictable results) — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on simple substitution of known elements yielding predictable results, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device/method/product differing from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have made the substitution and the results would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based factual findings are necessary for the case. If any of these findings cannot be made, the simple-substitution rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: In re Fout; In re O'Farrell; Agrizap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable results includes functioning for intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of a 'predictable result' covers not only that prior art elements can be physically combined, but also that the combination would have worked for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether combining elements would have produced the claimed function or purpose (DePuy example). Even if elements are physically combinable, a prior art teaching that combining would destroy an advantageous property or render the device inoperative (i.e., teaches away) weighs against an obviousness finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference 'teaches away' if it discourages, warns against, or shows that a proposed combination would be unsuitable or inoperative for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a primary reference teaches that a particular modification would be undesirable or would cause failure (e.g., Puno warning that increased rigidity increases failure), that reference may deter a person of ordinary skill from combining references. The totality of the prior art must be considered; teachings that warn of problems or adverse effects can support nonobviousness, and secondary considerations (failure by others, copying) can bolster that conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-to-be-solved approach in assessing analogous art and reason to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference from a different field is pertinent depends on the problem addressed: references addressing a similar problem may be analogous and may provide a reason to combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even references outside the inventor's field can be analogous if they address the same technical problem (ICON: Teague and ICON both address the need to stably retain a folding mechanism). Finding analogous art that addresses a similar problem 'goes a long way' toward demonstrating a reason to combine in obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifications a person skilled in the art would make
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying teachings from prior art, one must consider the reasonable modifications a person of ordinary skill would make in adapting a device from the prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that a borrowed device would be inoperable should account for the fact that a skilled artisan would size or modify components appropriately. An asserted inoperability cannot ignore plausible adaptations a skilled person would implement (ICON, Teague/ICON discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective evidence and nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) — such as commercial success, copying, praise, and failure by others — must have a nexus to the claimed features and be coextensive with the claims to be given weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of secondary considerations must be tied to the inventive features of the claim; lacking a proper nexus or coextensiveness reduces the weight accorded to such evidence (Muniauction: evidence lacked nexus and therefore was not entitled to substantial weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound / structural similarity in chemical cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical/pharmaceutical cases, proving obviousness from structural similarity requires showing some motivation that would have led a person of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound (a 'lead compound') and an expectation that the new compound would have similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation to modify may come from various sources and need not be explicit in the art; structural similarity can create an expectation of similar properties in light of the totality of the prior art (Aventis, Eisai). However, if modification would destroy an advantageous property or no reason to isolate/modify exists, the claim may be nonobvious (Eisai: no reason to modify lead compound because modification would destroy useful property).
